#9586. BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model

Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the Intended Use and Limitations for more information.

🤗 Model (safetensors)  |  📦 GGUFs (bf16, Q8, Q4)

We will take appropriate actions in response to notice of copyright infringement. If you believe your work has been used or copied in a manner that infringes upon your intellectual property rights, please email data-apps@tether.io identifying and describing both the copyrighted work and alleged infringing content to file a notice of infringement.

BotPsy is based on Qwen3.5-0.8B and is post-trained in four sequential stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and two rounds of Reinforcement Learning (RL). Each stage uses the previous stage's best checkpoint as its starting point and benefits from a different learning signal: imitation of reference trajectories, the token distributions of much larger teacher models, and rule-based tool-calling rewards (see Figure 3).

Our approach uses four stages of training, which learn from three types of signal: demonstrations, specialist teachers, and verifiable rewards.

We first perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on tool-use conversations. These include multi-turn agent trajectories from simulated environments, replayed single, parallel and multi-step calls, and cases where no tool should be called.

Next, the student is trained with on-policy distillation (OPD): it generates its own responses, and a specialist teacher provides feedback on every token, using the per-token reverse KL divergence as the training signal. To build the teachers, we first RL-trained three Qwen3.5-4B models to specialize in tool use, general reasoning, and instruction following. During training, every prompt is routed to one of these teachers. This stage mainly aims to recover knowledge and instruction following, which degraded during the SFT stage, although the tool-use metrics also increase (see Figure 4).

Learning from rules and environments (RL stages)

Finally, the model is trained with reinforcement learning using DAPO [1], learning only from rewards computed by rules and verifiers. The first round focuses on tool calling, accompanied by instruction following and STEM multiple-choice questions. As in Tool-N1 [2], the tool-calling reward first checks the reasoning and tool-call format. Instead of Tool-N1's binary correctness reward, however, it gives fine-grained partial credit in the spirit of ToolRL [3], matching the predicted tool names, argument names, and argument values against the ground truth.

The second round widens the training mix to general-domain verifiable tasks: math, code, knowledge (multiple-choice) questions, instruction following, structured outputs, and multi-step tool use in a simulated workplace environment. Although this mix contains no multi-turn conversations, it further improves multi-turn function calling.

Each stage of training uses a different data mixture (Figure 5). The SFT stage focuses mainly on tool use and prepares the ground for the subsequent stages. The MOPD mixture combines tool-use, knowledge and instruction-following data, both to further improve function calling and to recover the general-domain regressions from the SFT stage. The first RL stage again focuses mainly on tool use, while the second RL stage shifts the balance toward general-domain data (instruction following, knowledge, math and code), keeping a smaller share of tool use.

BotPsy roughly doubles the tool-use performance of its Qwen3.5-0.8B base and is the strongest of the five models on five of the six agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 23.4), ACEBench (58.7 vs 30.1), τ-bench (51.5 vs 23.2), BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 1.9) and ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 30.5). On all five, it is also ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size (37.7, 55.4, 46.5, 2.8 and 41.2 respectively; see Table 1). On Claw-Eval, Qwen3.5-2B-Think leads (48.9 vs 46.5).

Table 1: Tool-use and agentic benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined; multipliers give parameter count relative to BotPsy-0.8B. The average is the unweighted mean of the six benchmarks. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

Tool-use training did not cost general knowledge: GPQA Diamond rises from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9, the best of the models at 1.2B parameters or below (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35.0 and 39.4; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 15.8 and 40.0). Knowledge still scales mainly with parameter count, and Qwen3.5-2B-Think scores well above (59.9 and 65.5). BotPsy is therefore designed to call tools for facts it does not know, not to serve as a knowledge model.

Table 2: General-knowledge benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

BotPsy is the best of the five at following explicit instructions: IFEval 90.8 (base 59.7; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 80.0) and IFBench 55.9 (base 22.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 40.9). On Multi-IF, which tests instruction following over three turns in eight languages, it scores 67.2, on par with Qwen3.5-2B-Think (66.9) and LFM2.5-1.2B-Think (68.2). It starts strongest (84.3 in turn 1, the highest of the five) but drops faster as instructions accumulate (51.0 in turn 3, vs 56.5 and 56.2 for those two models). Lower-resource languages remain a weakness: Hindi (24.5) and Russian (57.6) are far below the 72–80 reached in English, Chinese, French, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese.

Table 3: Instruction-following benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

The largest relative gains come in multi-turn, stateful interaction, where BotPsy leads four of the five multi-turn benchmarks (Figure 6). On BFCL v4 multi-turn it rises from 7.5 to 46.1, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8), and on ACEBench Agent from 7.9 to 28.3 (Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 16.2). On τ²-bench it doubles its base in retail (67.8 vs 33.9, a narrow lead over Qwen3.5-2B-Think at 65.5) and reaches 82.5 in telecom, where the agent has to guide a user through troubleshooting over many turns (MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 74.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 69.3). It is also the most reliable of the five at single calls (BFCL non-live: 83.0) and at not calling a tool when none fits (BFCL hallucination: 86.1).

BotPsy's weaker spots are open-ended search and a few areas where Qwen3.5-2B-Think still leads. BotPsy's BrowseComp-Plus score of 4.5 is the best of the five, but low in absolute terms, and on BFCL web search (14.0) and memory (16.3) it trails Qwen3.5-2B-Think (19.8 and 26.1). On Claw-Eval, BotPsy improves clearly on its base (46.5 vs 39.3) but remains slightly below Qwen3.5-2B-Think (48.9). On ACEBench's special cases (incomplete or erroneous requests), Qwen3.5-2B-Think is also ahead (58.0 vs 51.3), although BotPsy is far above its base there (13.7). τ³-banking is the one multi-turn benchmark where BotPsy does not lead: no model gets above 5 (BotPsy 4.1, unchanged from its base; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 4.8).

BotPsy can handle a variety of use cases and scenarios. Figure 7 breaks the benchmark scenarios down by app group, separating simple scenarios (single turn, one tool call) from complex ones (multi-turn or multi-tool). The overall scores quoted in this section are averaged over all scenarios; the bottom row of Figure 7 is an unweighted mean of the seven groups, so its numbers differ.

Simple scenarios score 70–79 in every app group with a meaningful sample (Communication & Social has only 6). Overall, BotPsy scores 75, about 21 points above its base model (54) and slightly above Qwen3.5-2B-Think (70).

On complex scenarios, BotPsy scores 39.5 overall, against 17.9 for its base and 30.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. The gain is largest in Communication & Social (61 vs 13 for the base), Commerce & Services (58 vs 27) and Device & System Management (46 vs 15). Qwen3.5-2B-Think is ahead only in Personal Productivity & Work (64 vs 58, 38 scenarios, mostly Claw-Eval), and MiniCPM5-1B-Think is marginally ahead in Communication & Social (61.5 vs 60.5). Multi-step tasks still score lower than single calls, which remains the main limit for harder tasks.

Complex Information Retrieval & Research scenarios score 15 (single calls: 79). Most are BrowseComp-Plus deep-research questions, which stay hard for every model in this size range (base: 9; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 14).

BotPsy reaches correct answers with much less reasoning than its base, and with fewer turns on multi-turn agent tasks. This aligns with our explicit focus on reasoning efficiency throughout training. All comparisons below are made on the same questions or tasks (those that all five models answered correctly or solved), so differences in difficulty do not drive the numbers. Reasoning tokens are counted with each model's own tokenizer.

Shorter reasoning, with higher accuracy. Compared with its base, BotPsy uses 1.4–3.1× fewer reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563), MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105), IFEval (3,148 vs 4,433) and IFBench (4,204 vs 11,576), while scoring higher on all four (Figure 8). It is not the shortest model everywhere: LFM2.5-1.2B-Think writes shorter reasoning on MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench, and MiniCPM5-1B-Think on IFEval and IFBench, but at lower accuracy than BotPsy on each.

Fewer turns than the base on multi-turn agent tasks. On τ²-bench tasks that all five models solve, BotPsy needs fewer assistant turns than its base (Figure 9):

It does this while passing 2.0× (retail) and 2.6× (telecom) as many tasks as the base. MiniCPM5-1B-Think uses fewer turns on retail (8.7), but passes only 9.9% of retail tasks.

BotPsy has been developed to advance the state of the art and to support research and educational uses. Models developed based on our work could be suitable for tasks in domains such as device & system management (settings, files & documents, clocks & alarms), personal productivity & work (calendar & tasks, email, collaboration tools), communication (messaging), information retrieval & research (web search, weather, news), media & lifestyle (video, music, recipes & fitness, photos) and commerce & services (maps & travel, finance, shopping & delivery). Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty.

BotPsy has been primarily trained and tested in English, which is the recommended language. It has also been evaluated on Multi-IF, which covers seven additional languages (Chinese, French, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish): it performs well in most of them, but scores much lower in Hindi and Russian. BotPsy is a small language model, and it makes mistakes. It is not intended for safety-critical or high-stakes automated decisions, or for applications involving money, personal information, health and other sensitive topics.

[1] Yu, Qiying, et al. "DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (2025): 113222–113244.

[2] Zhang, Shaokun, et al. "Nemotron-Research-Tool-N1: Exploring Tool-Using Language Models with Reinforced Reasoning." International Conference on Learning Representations (2026).

[3] Qian, Cheng, et al. "ToolRL: Reward is All Tool Learning Needs." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (2025).

#9581. Running an MCP server behind a secret URL

Posted on Nov 11 • Originally published at richardlemon.com

This pattern runs a stdio MCP server on a small VPS and makes it reachable from Claude via an MCP gateway, without exposing the raw stdio server to the internet or wiring up OAuth.

The unusual part is that the only practical authentication ends up being a long, unguessable URL path.

The Claude connectors for MCP give you two options for talking to a remote HTTP endpoint:

There is no option to attach arbitrary headers. No API key header, no HMAC, nothing you can control at the HTTP level apart from the URL itself.

That constraint rules out the usual pattern of putting a shared secret in a header and validating it at the gateway or proxy. If you want header-based auth, you have to put something in front of the MCP endpoint that can enforce it before traffic ever reaches the connector-facing URL.

For a small, private tool, OAuth is often heavier than the rest of the stack combined. If you do not want to run an OAuth provider or wire into an existing one, the remaining option inside the connector model is to treat the URL path as a secret:

In that setup the URL path behaves like a shared secret. If someone has it, they can reach the server. If they do not, they have no obvious handle to brute-force, as long as the path has enough entropy.

This is not ideal security. It is security-by-entropy, with the usual caveats. Given the connector constraints, the trade-off is between:

The stdio MCP server runs as a process. The gateway talks to it over stdio. HTTP, nginx, and the MCP gateway all think in slightly different units: requests, connections, and sessions.

Many gateway setups lean toward a model of “one process per session.” Each new MCP session from Claude can spin up a fresh process for the tool server. On a small droplet with limited RAM, that is not just a theoretical concern. Multiple active sessions mean multiple processes and real memory pressure.

Running the MCP server under its own user as a systemd service limits the blast radius, but does not remove the underlying constraint. If you adopt this pattern, plan for:

When the URL path is the only secret, every place that path appears becomes a potential leak. nginx access logs are a common example.

By default, every request to the secret path lands in access_log. That means:

A simple mitigation is to turn off access logging for the specific location that fronts the MCP gateway:

Error logs can stay on, because they are useful when something is broken, but the normal request flow should leave as little trace as possible if the URL is acting as your auth.

Because the URL path is doing more work than it should, everything around it benefits from being tighter:

None of this turns the setup into a high-assurance security boundary, but it does reduce the impact of mistakes in any single layer.

This structure is only a good fit in a narrow set of cases:

In that scenario, the trade-off is straightforward: a private remote MCP tool without building a full auth system or running extra infrastructure, in exchange for accepting that the URL is doing more security work than it should.

There are also clear cases where this pattern is the wrong choice:

In those situations, invest in real authentication. Use OAuth, or put the MCP gateway behind something that can enforce headers, tokens, or mutual TLS before traffic ever reaches it.

A small droplet with a secret path can be acceptable for a personal tool you are willing to babysit. Once it grows beyond that, the shortcuts stop being shortcuts.

#9577. One Prompt, Every Log: Triage Production Issues Faster with MCP

Production issues aren't painful because fixing bugs is hard. They're painful because finding where the bug originated can take hours.

This is where MCP (Model Context Protocol) comes in. MCP is an open standard that allows AI assistants to connect with external tools and data sources, such as databases, monitoring platforms, application logs, and project management tools. It enables AI to interact with these systems and gather the context needed to investigate complex issues.

Hi I'm Shakti, a Software Engineer at a bug healthcare company. Recently I've been working closely with production issues and I've realized one thing time is everything when dealing with production incidents.

The real challenge isn't just fixing the bug. It's identifying where it originated, performing Root Cause Analysis (RCA), and reproducing the issue in lower environments.

All these steps can be extremely time-consuming.

Here are some practical tips on how you can use AI to triage production issues faster, identify root causes, and save valuable debugging time.

Start by identifying all the tools you manually use while triaging production issues.

Basically think about every tool you manually open when investigating a production issue and check whether an MCP is available for it.

Having an MCP integration doesn't automatically mean you have access to everything.

Check whether your account has the required permissions to access these tools, especially production databases, monitoring dashboards, application logs, and Jira projects.

Make sure you follow your organization's security and access policies. Prefer read-only access wherever possible.

Once you've identified the required MCP servers and verified your permissions, connect them to your primary AI harness or the AI assistant you use daily.

For example, this could be Claude, Cursor, or another AI environment that supports MCP integrations.

Now that you've connected all the tools, verify that your AI assistant can actually communicate with them.

Don't move forward until you've verified that the integrations are working as expected.

Create a separate project in your AI harness specifically for production issue triaging.

Give this project a detailed system prompt that defines the AI's role as an experienced Production Support Engineer who understands debugging, root cause analysis, log investigation, and issue reproduction.

Important: Instruct the AI not to assume a root cause without evidence. It should clearly distinguish confirmed findings from hypotheses.

Simply take the Jira ticket associated with the production issue and pass it to your dedicated AI project.

Your AI assistant can start investigating the issue using all the connected MCP tools, correlate information across different systems, and generate an investigation report.

Instead of manually switching between Jira, Grafana, databases, and log management platforms, you now have one place to coordinate the investigation.

The goal isn't to replace your debugging skills with AI. It's to eliminate repetitive investigation work so you can focus on understanding and resolving the actual problem.

AI won't magically fix every production issue, but with the right MCP integrations, context, and instructions, it can significantly reduce the time spent on investigation and debugging.

Stop spending hours collecting logs and switching between tools. Start using AI to connect the dots.

#9575. How long does pie last in the fridge? : Because we're all wondering what to do with our apple and pumpkin pies.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions. Today: How long does pie last in the fridge?

The season of plentiful pies is upon us. When preparing several pies for a holiday meal, you may be wondering about the imminent leftovers. Should apple pie be stored differently than pumpkin pie? David from our Baker’s Hotline is here with his expert advice to help.

“Baked apple or other fruit pies can be kept covered, at room temperature, for one to two days. After that, they’ll keep in the fridge for one to two more days,” David advises. A 15-minute reheat in a 350°F oven can help revive some of that freshly baked flavor. Tent the pie with foil so it doesn’t brown further.

Interested in prepping ahead? David says that storing an assembled, ready-to-bake apple pie is a bad idea; the fruity filling will release moisture, which will make your crust soggy. Instead, roll out your pie crusts and prep your apples, but keep them separate. And wait to add the sugar and spices to the apples until you’re ready to bake the pie. This way, you can pour off any liquid that’s accumulated from the fruit without draining off your thickener, sugar, and spices.

Sliced apples turn brown, so you don’t want to keep your prepared apples in the fridge very long before baking. Aim for under 24 hours, but a squeeze of lemon juice could help them last another day or so.

And if you want to use your freezer to prep ahead, here’s how to freeze and bake fruit pies.

David advises, “Baked pumpkin pie or other pies containing eggs and/or dairy such as pecan pie, custard pie, or chiffon pie should be stored refrigerated; they’ll keep in the fridge for three to four days. I like to transfer the pie to a shallow, lidded storage container, but plastic wrap or a storage top can be used as well.”

As with apple, if you’re making your pumpkin (and other custard) pie ahead, it’s best to keep filling and crust separate. Pumpkin pie filling can be made ahead; it’ll keep, refrigerated, overnight. In fact, that's actually what we recommend doing; the custard develops incredible flavor and aroma as it sits.

If you can, serve pies the day they were made instead of refrigerating them.

Reheat refrigerated pies in a 350°F oven for about 15 minutes prior to serving.

Apple and other fruit pies will last at room temperature for up to two days, then in the fridge for two more.

Pumpkin, custard, or other egg/dairy-based pies can be stored in the fridge for up to four days.

If you’re making the crust and the filling ahead, keep them separated until it’s time to bake your pie.

#9572. Who Should Get AI Coding Tools at Work?

Posted on Nov 11 • Originally published at ksofttechnologies.com

Giving everyone the newest AI coding agent sounds progressive.

It can also create a situation where people generate code they cannot review, tools reach data they should not see, and nobody knows whether the productivity gain is real.

Give people the AI capability their job requires, under controls appropriate to what that capability can access and change.

The recent Goldman Sachs story is a useful example.

Bloomberg reported on November 2, 2026 that internal guidance updated in October restricted Anthropic's Claude Code and Microsoft's GitHub coding tools for most bankers and traders, while engineers retained access. The directive reportedly did not apply to "strats," whose work spans trading, quantitative research, and software engineering. Goldman said it experiments with tools across the firm and considers factors including productivity and risk management before deciding who is best suited to use them longer term.

The lesson is that AI access can be role-based instead of universal.

What does this role actually need to accomplish?

An engineer may reasonably need an agent that can inspect a repository, generate tests, modify files, or prepare a pull request.

Someone in another department may get more value from an assistant that can summarize documents, draft content, or analyze approved information.

They do not require identical permissions.

The mistake is treating the most powerful tier as the default.

"AI tool" is becoming too broad a category.

Calling both "coding assistants" hides the important difference.

READ What can it see? WRITE What can it change? EXECUTE What can it run? DEPLOY Can it affect production? TRANSACT Can it trigger business actions?

Each step increases the control requirements.

A tool that generates a function inside an IDE is one thing.

An agent with credentials, terminal access, and deployment permissions is another.

This is where broad access becomes uncomfortable.

AI can let someone generate code they could not have written independently.

That does not mean they can evaluate it independently.

Generated code can look perfectly reasonable while containing:

For production-impacting work, I want someone involved who can recognize those problems.

That does not mean non-developers should never experiment with code.

It means experimentation should not automatically grant production authority.

If someone cannot meaningfully review what the agent creates, another qualified person should.

Companies often jump between two extremes:

Sandbox ↓ Limited repository ↓ Human-reviewed changes ↓ Controlled production use

During the pilot, measure actual work rather than enthusiasm.

Did unexpected data-access issues appear?

A pilot tells you whether it belongs in your operating environment.

Most AI security problems do not require malicious employees.

A normal employee can accidentally paste the wrong information into the wrong tool.

That is why "use common sense" is a weak AI policy.

At minimum, employees should know how the company treats:

customer data credentials API keys private source code financial records internal documents regulated information production data

Then support policy with technical controls where possible:

SSO role-based permissions approved integrations repository restrictions secret scanning audit logs revocable access

The policy should tell people what is allowed.

The architecture should make the dangerous path harder.

This may become the most important governance habit.

A tool approved six months ago as autocomplete may later gain:

repository-wide context file modification command execution browser access pull request creation external integrations agentic workflows

Now the approval describes the actual capability.

Typical / indicative only. My rough read is that capability, verification, and data access deserve more attention than simply deciding whether a product is "approved."

Before approving a coding tool, I would ask:

[ ] What job requires it? [ ] What data can it read? [ ] What systems can it modify? [ ] Can it execute commands? [ ] Can it reach production? [ ] Who verifies its output? [ ] What requires human approval? [ ] Are actions logged? [ ] Can access be revoked quickly? [ ] What is the worst plausible mistake? [ ] What will success be measured against?

A tool that generates code in seconds but creates an hour of cleanup has not necessarily improved productivity.

How KSoft Technologies Helps With Responsible AI Adoption

KSoft Technologies is our own software engineering company. We help teams evaluate AI-assisted development and automation in the context of their existing architecture, permissions, integrations, review processes, and data boundaries rather than treating the tool as an isolated purchase.

The question I would ask every technical leader is:

Which person needs which capability, against which systems, with what review?

That produces a much better policy than either "everyone gets AI" or "nobody gets AI."

I wrote the longer version here: Who Should Get AI Coding Tools at Work?.

#9570. The draw is 24% of the outcomes and 0.8% of the labels: auditing class collapse in a three-way model

Posted on Nov 11 • Originally published at soccerdreamai.com

A three-class classifier that reports one label per row is not a three-class classifier. It is a ranking function collapsed to a decision, and the collapse is where the information dies. On our platform, 11,177 of 46,189 settled predictions ended in a draw; the label draw was emitted 360 times.

Every number below comes from the live production table, queried today, not estimated.

The base table stores one row per model per match with the realised outcome attached. Two distributions matter: what happened, and what the model said would happen. If the second is a faithful compression of the first, they should be close.

The draw happens 24.20% of the time and is named as the sole answer 0.78% of the time — a 31× under-representation. 16,925 rows name it as one of two outcomes; 27,647 rows chose strictly between home and away and could not be correct if the match finished level.

That last set is the interesting one. Of those 27,647 binary picks, 6,269 (22.68%) finished level. The ceiling was set by the label vocabulary, not the analysis.

Reported accuracy by output arity on rows with a settled outcome:

58.52% on single-label rows looks like a margin over chance. But chance for a 44/31/24 class split under a majority-class strategy is 44.26% — and the "single" bucket is not homogeneous: 4,490 of those rows had a compound single label (home/draw, away/draw) and 27,647 were strictly two-class. Averaging them reports neither.

This is a binary classifier wearing a three-class schema: any binary classifier over football outcomes pays a fixed 22.68% tax on the subset it is applied to. A genuine three-class system moves that tax into calibrated probability on the draw.

Aggregate accuracy is what lets this bug live for 46,000 rows. Per-class precision and recall make it visible in one screen:

Result on the 45,860 rows with a non-null outcome:

Draw precision of 26.81% hides the shape of the failure: draw alone hit 78 of 360 (21.67%), while away/draw hit 5,920 of 10,997 (53.83%) and home/draw hit 3,272 of 5,928 (55.20%). The compound labels are not predicting a draw — they express uncertainty between two outcomes, and the draw is an escape hatch. Recall on the draw is 41.16%: 6,576 draws were named by no label at all.

The most damning row: 283 distinct models emitted draw at least once across 46,189 predictions, and the busiest did it 4 times. No model here has learned to identify draws. Some occasionally guess.

Accuracy cannot compare a one-hot label with a distribution. Log loss can. The emitted label is scored as a probability vector (1.0 on the named class, split evenly for compounds) against the market-implied probability from the quoted three-way price, normalised to sum to one. 45,110 of 46,189 rows survive the price sanity filter.

Log loss 0.9683 for the market-implied probabilities, 13.4625 for the emitted label — a factor of 13.9. That is what a zero looks like inside a logarithm: every row where the model picked a compound and the outcome was the excluded class contributes -log(0), clamped at 1e-12, or 27.6 nats.

This is not a claim that market probabilities are a good model. It is a claim about representation: a probability vector can be scored and improved; a one-hot label can only be counted, and counting rewards the majority class. The draw Brier of 0.1812 is what a real three-class output would have to beat.

If confidence carried draw-risk signal, high-confidence binary picks would convert to draws less often. They don't. Draw rate among single picks restricted to home or away (27,647 rows, 6,269 draws):

Flat, and mildly inverted at the top: a model that says 9 is no less likely to be level than one that says 4. That is the expected failure when confidence is attached to a binary comparison and the third class was pruned before scoring — the pruning discards the evidence.

The market-implied draw probability, on the same 45,110 rows, is calibrated in the ordinary sense:

Mean implied 0.2423 against an observed 24.20%. The information is already in a column we store, and it is thrown away at the label step.

Draw rates are not uniform across competitions. On 78,553 finished matches the overall draw rate is 24.69% (19,392 draws), and competition buckets with at least 500 settled rows span 15.49% to 30.42%:

A single global threshold for "is this a draw?" is therefore wrong by about 15 percentage points. A per-class correction must be conditioned on the competition, and that requires a calibrated probability rather than a relabelled decision — you cannot attach a competition prior to a one-hot output.

The 46,189 settled predictions cover 16,724 distinct matches, and only 3,736 (8.09%) join to matches on id; the rest carry a match_id from an older identifier space. Every per-competition number above was computed from matches directly — joining predictions to competitions would have dropped 92% of rows and produced a confident, wrong table.

Second: 329 settled rows have actual_result IS NULL and 121 have hit IS NULL while settled is true. They are excluded explicitly with FILTER.

A 24% versus 0.8% gap is not a dataset problem. Twenty-four percent is an ordinary share for the third class of a football outcome. The imbalance was manufactured by the output format: the model emitted a label, the vocabulary had three slots, and the scoring loop only rewarded the slot that appeared most. Fixing it needs no better model — three numbers instead of one string, and a refusal to ship a three-class system whose per-class recall is never measured for one of its classes.

The draw was never hard to predict. It was hard to record.

Analytics and research content. Not betting advice. 18+

#9569. Top 10 AI Tools in 2023 That Will Make Your Life Easier



 In this article, we explore the top 10 AI tools that are driving innovation and efficiency in various industries. These tools are designed to automate repetitive tasks, improve workflow, and increase productivity. The tools included in our list are some of the most advanced and widely used in the market, and are suitable for a variety of applications. Some of the tools focus on natural language processing, such as ChatGPT and Grammarly, while others focus on image and video generation, such as DALL-E and Lumen5. Other tools such as OpenAI Codex, Tabnine, Canva, Jasper AI,, and Surfer SEO are designed to help with specific tasks such as code understanding content writing and website optimization. This list is a great starting point for anyone looking to explore the possibilities of AI and how it can be applied to their business or project.

So let’s dive into

1. ChatGPT

ChatGPT is a large language model that generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts. It can be used for tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion. It can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing, and generates coherent and fluent text, but should be used with care as it may generate text that is biased, offensive, or factually incorrect.

Pros:

  • Generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts
  • Can be fine-tuned for specific tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion
  • Can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing
  • Can generate coherent and fluent text, even when completing a given text prompt.

Cons:

  • May generate text that is biased or offensive
  • Can generate text that is not accurate or factually correct
  • May require large amounts of computational resources to run
  • The model can sometimes generate text that is not coherent or fluent, depending on the prompt given.

Overall, ChatGPT is a powerful tool for natural language processing, but it should be used with care and with an understanding of its limitations.

2. DALL-E

DALL-E is a generative model developed by OpenAI that is capable of generating images from text prompts. It is based on the GPT-3 architecture, which is a transformer-based neural network language model that has been trained on a massive dataset of text. DALL-E can generate images that are similar to a training dataset and it can generate high-resolution images that are suitable for commercial use.

Pros:

  • Generates high-resolution images
  • Can generate images from text prompts
  • It can be fine-tuned for specific tasks such as generating images of a certain style or category

Cons:

  • May generate images that are not entirely original and could be influenced by the training data
  • May require significant computational resources to run
  • The quality of the generated images may vary depending on the specific prompt

Overall, DALL-E is a powerful AI-based tool for generating images, it can be used for a variety of applications such as creating images for commercial use, gaming, and other creative projects. It is important to note that the generated images should be reviewed and used with care, as they may not be entirely original and could be influenced by the training data.

3. Lumen5

Lumen5 is a content creation platform that uses AI to help users create videos, social media posts, and other types of content. It has several features that make it useful for content creation and marketing, including:

Pros:

  • Automatically summarizes text from a blog post, article, or another source into a script for a video or social media post
  • Offers a library of royalty-free videos, images, and music to use in content
  • Has a drag-and-drop interface for easy content creation
  • Can create videos in multiple languages
  • Has a built-in analytics tool to track the performance of created content.

Cons:

  • The quality of the generated content may vary depending on the source material
  • The automatic summarization feature may not always capture the main points of the source material
  • The library of videos, images, and music is limited.
  • The analytics feature is basic

Overall, Lumen5 is a useful tool for creating content quickly and easily, it can help automate the process of creating videos, social media posts, and other types of content. However, the quality of the generated content may vary depending on the source material and it is important to review and edit the content before publishing it.

4. Grammarly

Grammarly is a writing-enhancement platform that uses AI to check for grammar, punctuation, and spelling errors in the text. It also provides suggestions for improving the clarity, concision, and readability of the text. It has several features that make it useful for improving writing, including:

Pros:

  • Checks for grammar, punctuation, and spelling errors in the text
  • Provides suggestions for improving clarity, concision, and readability
  • Can be integrated with various apps and platforms such as Microsoft Office, Google Docs, and social media platforms
  • Offers a browser extension and a desktop app
  • Has a premium version with more advanced features such as plagiarism detection and more

Cons:

  • The suggestions provided may not always be accurate or appropriate
  • The grammar checker may not always recognize context-specific language use
  • The free version has limited features
  • Limited to English language only
  • Overall, Grammarly is a useful tool for improving writing, it can help users identify and correct grammar and punctuation errors, and improve the clarity, concision, and readability of their text. However, it is important to review the suggestions provided by the tool and use them with caution, as they may not always be accurate or appropriate.

5.OpenAI Codex

OpenAI Codex is a system developed by OpenAI that can create code from natural language descriptions of software tasks. The system is based on the GPT-3 model and can generate code in multiple programming languages.

Pros:

  • Can automate the process of writing code
  • Can help developers to be more productive
  • Can help non-technical people to create software
  • Can generate code in multiple programming languages

Cons:

  • The quality of the generated code may vary depending on the task description
  • The generated code may not always be optimal or efficient
  • The system may not be able to handle complex software tasks
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the code.

Overall, OpenAI Codex is a powerful tool that can help automate the process of writing code and make it more accessible to non-technical people. However, the quality of the generated code may vary depending on the task description and it is important to review and test the code before using it in a production environment. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the developer's knowledge.

6. Tabnine

Tabnine is a code completion tool that uses AI to predict and suggest code snippets. It is compatible with multiple programming languages and can be integrated with various code editors.

Pros:

  • Can improve coding efficiency by suggesting code snippets based on context
  • Can complete entire code blocks
  • Can predict variables, functions, and other elements of code
  • Can be integrated with various code editors

Cons:

  • The suggestions may not always be accurate or appropriate
  • The system may not always be able to understand the context of the code
  • May not work with all code editors
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the code.

Overall, TabNine is a useful tool for developers that can help improve coding efficiency and reduce the time spent on writing code. However, it is important to review the suggestions provided by the tool and use them with caution, as they may not always be accurate or appropriate. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the developer's knowledge.

7. Jasper AI

Jasper is a content writing and content generation tool that uses artificial intelligence to identify the best words and sentences for your writing style and medium in the most efficient, quick, and accessible way.

Pros:

  • User-friendly interface
  • Generates a wide variety of content types
  • Guarantees 100% unique and free-plagiarism content
  • SEO friendly
  •  Create articles of up to 10k words

Cons:

  • Not the cheapest AI writer on the market

8. Surfer SEO

Surfer SEO is a software tool designed to help website owners and digital marketers improve their search engine optimization (SEO) efforts. The tool provides a variety of features that can be used to analyze a website's on-page SEO, including:

Features:

  • A site audit tool that checks for technical SEO issues
  • A content editor that suggests optimizations for individual pages
  • A keyword research tool that suggests keywords to target
  • A SERP analyzer that shows how a website's pages rank for specific keywords
  • A backlink analysis tool that shows the backlinks pointing to a website.

Pros:

  • Can help website owners and marketers identify technical SEO issues
  • Can provide suggestions for optimizing individual pages
  • Can help with keyword research
  • Can show how a website's pages rank for specific keywords
  • Can provide insight into a website's backlink profile

Cons:

  • Some features may require a paid subscription
  • The tool is not a guarantee of better ranking
  • The tool can only analyze the data it has access to
  • The tool's suggestions may not always be applicable or optimal

Overall, Surfer SEO can be a useful tool for website owners and digital marketers looking to improve their SEO efforts. However, it is important to remember that it is just a tool and should be used in conjunction with other SEO best practices. Additionally, the tool is not a guarantee of better ranking.

9. Zapier

Zapier is a web automation tool that allows users to automate repetitive tasks by connecting different web applications together. It does this by creating "Zaps" that automatically move data between apps, and can also be used to trigger certain actions in one app based on events in another app.

Features:

  • Can connect over 3,000 web applications
  • Can automate repetitive tasks
  • Can create "Zaps" to move data between apps
  • Can trigger certain actions in one app based on events in another app.

Pros:

  • Can automate repetitive tasks
  • Can save time
  • Can improve workflow
  • Can increase productivity
  • Can be integrated with a wide range of web applications

Cons:

  • Can be difficult to set up
  • May require some technical skills
  • May require a paid subscription for some features
  • Some apps may not be compatible
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the apps

Overall, Zapier is a useful tool that can help users automate repetitive tasks and improve workflow. It can save time and increase productivity by connecting different web applications together. However, it may require some technical skills and some features may require a paid subscription. It is important to use the tool with caution and not to rely too much on it, to understand the apps better.

10. Compose AI

Compose AI is a company that specializes in developing natural language generation (NLG) software. Their software uses AI to automatically generate written or spoken text from structured data, such as spreadsheets, databases, or APIs.

Features:

  • Automatically generates written or spoken text from structured data
  • Can be integrated with a wide range of data sources
  • Can be used for a variety of applications such as creating reports, summaries, and explanations
  • Provides an API and a user-friendly interface

Pros:

  • Can automate the process of creating written or spoken content
  • Can help users create more accurate and consistent content
  • Can help users save time by automating repetitive tasks
  • Can be integrated with a wide range of data sources

Cons:

  • The quality of the generated content may vary depending on the data source
  • The generated content may not always be optimal or efficient
  • The system may not be able to handle complex tasks
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the data

Overall, Compose AI's NLG software can be a useful tool for automating the process of creating written or spoken content from structured data. However, the quality of the generated content may vary depending on the data source, and it is essential to review the generated content before using it in a production environment. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the understanding of the data.

Conclusion

AI tools are becoming increasingly important in today's business and technology landscape. They are designed to automate repetitive tasks, improve workflow, and increase productivity. The top 10 AI tools included in this article are some of the most advanced and widely used in the market, and are suitable for various applications. Whether you're looking to improve your natural language processing, create high-resolution images, or optimize your website, there is an AI tool that can help. It's important to research and evaluate the different tools available to determine which one is the best fit for your specific needs. As AI technology continues to evolve, these tools will become even more powerful and versatile and will play an even greater role in shaping the future of business and technology.

#9566. Reddit Reviews Landed With 161 Comments and Zero Upvotes

Reddit's announcement post for Reddit Reviews is sitting at zero votes. The comment section under it has 161 replies.

That ratio is the review. Zero up, 161 down.

And it was written by the people who actually run the site's communities.

The feature is simple enough. Reddit used AI to pull product talk from across subreddits and pack it into about 10,000 product pages. Electronics, health and beauty, home and garden, apparel, US only.

You search a product, and you get a "what people are saying" block. Positive, mixed, negative split, plus topic filters.

And every summary links back to the original threads.

Fine idea on paper. Reddit has been the place people go to ask whether an air fryer is worth it for a decade. This just puts a label on it.

The top one, at 114 points, is from a user called judasblue. "Yeah, this definitely isn't going to lead to even more fake account stealth marketing efforts across the site."

"Oh those advertising spam accounts are giving you consistent issues? What if instead of dealing with them we intentionally built them features to make THEIR jobs easier?"

That is the mood. Not curiosity. Not "cool, shopping."

Just a long tired sigh from people who spend their evenings deleting bots.

i went looking for the beta timeline first, because it explains a lot. Reddit tested this since February with a small group of US users in electronics, video games, and health and beauty.

And in September it added home and garden plus apparel. Now it is open to every US user.

There is also product info with images, prices, and where to buy links. Reddit says that data comes from brand and retailer catalogs. The early testing ran in places like r/espresso and r/skincareaddiction, where people already argue about grinders and moisturizer for free.

That last part is what nobody in the thread liked. Price and buy links turn a conversation into a store shelf.

brandy_mcstyle from Reddit's product marketing team answered concerns directly in the thread. The defense has two parts.

Reddit excludes comments from accounts labeled as apps. And it defines a "review conversation" as a comment that appears to describe personal experience with a product.

A user named DeltaJesus replied with the obvious thing.

"So exactly what these bots are already doing now?"

He is right. Astroturfing has never looked like a press release.

It looks like a person saying they owned the thing for six months and it changed their life. Filtering for personal experience filters for the exact shape of a paid comment.

Reddit's answer to fake reviews is a detector tuned to copy the fakes.

Four separate mods asked how to turn this off for their subreddits. Beeb294, Sillvaro, SecureThruObscure, and LindyNet all wanted an off switch. None of them got one.

judasblue asked the sharper version. If Reddit is not making money from this feature, why not let non commercial subs opt out? He called the absence of a switch "sus," which is about as polite as that thread gets.

CouncilOfStrongs, a mod of over ten years, put the trust problem in one line. "There has been zero noticeable reduction in spam volume in the over 10 years I have been a moderator on this platform."

And WalkingEars added the detail that stings. Subs without aggressive moderation are now full of "insipid LLM posts that read more like LinkedIn than Reddit."

Follow the money, or the missing money. Reddit's shares dropped 29% after investors got spooked about Google's AI Overviews eating referral traffic from search. The company is also moving toward a logged in experience, which keeps people on site instead of letting search engines index everything for free.

Reddit Reviews lands weeks later, right before holiday shopping. That timing is not subtle.

Reddit also says it earns no commission on those buy links. Maybe true today. A shopping surface with 130 million daily users and live price data does not usually stay commission free for long.

The line that stuck with me is buried in the announcement. Half of US shoppers say they come to Reddit to validate AI recommendations.

Read that twice. People ask a model for advice, then come to Reddit to check whether the model lied. Reddit's new feature hands them an AI summary of the human answers they came for.

The loop closes on itself. Ask a model, verify with a model that read people, then buy.

i do not think Reddit is evil for this. i think it is a company with a traffic problem building a shopping product, because shopping products make money.

But the packaging is what annoys me. This is not a community tool. It is a storefront wearing a community tool's jacket.

Somewhere in the middle of all this i remembered my own review habit. i read the two star reviews first, always. Not the one stars, those are people having a bad day with a delivery driver.

The two stars are where the real complaints live. The hinge that loosened after four months. The app that stopped syncing.

And i once spent forty minutes in a rice cooker thread because one commenter had measured the actual temperature variance across three units with a probe. No brand. No affiliate link.

Just a guy with a thermometer and a grudge.

That is the thing Reddit Reviews cannot summarize. The grudge. The guy who measured.

A summary keeps the verdict and throws away the obsession that made it worth reading.

If you already search Reddit by adding "reddit" to your Google query, this feature is not for you. You will find the thread anyway, and you will read the messy parts that a summary flattens.

If you are the kind of shopper who reads one product page and calls it research, this will feel like a shortcut. And it mostly is one, for better and worse.

The people who should actually care are the mods. They get the spam risk, the extra moderation load, and no switch to turn any of it off. The feature benefits the shopper who never opens Reddit and costs the volunteer who keeps it usable.

That trade is bad. Not complicated. Just bad.

The comment i keep coming back to is from TGotAReddit, replying to Reddit's claim that nobody pays for placement. "Well if you don't benefit and the advertisers don't benefit, who does this benefit? Because it's not gonna help mods or users."

i keep thinking about the zero votes. Reddit built a review machine for ten thousand products and its own users could not bring themselves to click the up arrow on the announcement.

Maybe that is the most honest review on the page.

#9563. Progressive Web Apps vs Native App: When a PWA Is Enough

Posted on Nov 11 • Originally published at muhammadmoiz.dev

Originally published at muhammadmoiz.dev.

If you are weighing progressive web apps vs native app development, the short answer is this: a PWA is enough when your users mostly work in the foreground, on screens you control, and you need one codebase with fast updates. Go native (or React Native) when you depend on background work, deep hardware access, or iOS features that Safari still does not expose. Below is how to tell which side of that line your product sits on, based on current browser support data and on building an offline-first restaurant POS that runs in the browser.

A progressive web app is a website that can behave like an installed app. Technically it is still a web page running inside a browser engine, but it adds two things:

Once installed, a PWA gets its own icon and opens in its own window without the browser address bar. To the user it feels like an app. Under the hood, the browser is still doing the work, and that is the root of every limitation discussed below.

A native app, by contrast, is built for the operating system directly (Swift/Kotlin, or a cross-platform toolkit like React Native or Flutter that compiles to native components) and is distributed through the App Store or Google Play.

The rows that matter most are the bottom four. Everything above them is where PWAs usually win.

Most "PWA vs native" decisions are really "how much do we care about iPhone users?" decisions. Android with Chrome supports far more of the web platform than iOS does. I checked MDN's browser compatibility data in November 2026, and these are the gaps that most often push a project toward native:

Safari on iOS added the Push API in version 16.4, but MDN notes it only works for web apps saved to the Home Screen. A user who just visits your site in Safari cannot get push messages. That means your onboarding has to talk people through "Share, then Add to Home Screen" before notifications even become possible.

On Chrome and Edge, your app can listen for the beforeinstallprompt event and show its own "Install app" button at a sensible moment. Safari does not support that event, and MDN states plainly that this technique does not work on iOS. Installing is entirely manual for iPhone users. Since iOS 16.4, they can at least do it from the Share menu in Safari, Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Orion, not only Safari.

The Background Synchronization API lets a service worker retry a failed request once the connection returns, even after the user has closed the tab. Periodic Background Sync and Background Fetch go further. According to MDN's compatibility data, Safari supports none of these. On iOS, your app can only sync while it is open.

Web Bluetooth, WebUSB and Web Serial exist in Chromium browsers but not in Safari. If your product needs to talk to a card reader, label printer, scale or other peripheral from an iPhone or iPad, a PWA alone cannot do it.

Check the EU caveat: Historically every iOS browser had to use WebKit, so Chrome on iPhone had Safari's limits. MDN notes that since iOS 17.4 Apple allows other browser engines in the EU, so behaviour there can differ. Test on the devices and regions your customers actually use.

Offline-first apps live or die on local storage, so this deserves its own section. Small key-value data can go in localStorage, which is capped at about 5 MiB per origin. Anything serious (orders, products, customers) belongs in IndexedDB, usually through a library rather than the raw API.

MDN's storage guide gives the current quota rules:

The bigger risk is not quota, it is eviction. By default, browser data is "best-effort", meaning the browser may delete it under storage pressure. Safari goes further: with cross-site tracking prevention on, it removes script-created data for origins the user has not interacted with in the last seven days of browser use. When eviction happens, the whole origin's data goes at once.

And the rule that matters more than any API call: local data must never be the only copy of anything important. Sync it to a server as soon as a connection is available, and design the app so a wiped device can rebuild itself from the server.

I spent about two years as a senior frontend engineer on Oscar, a point of sale system for restaurants and retail in Pakistan. It is a React web app, not a store app, and it had to keep taking orders, printing receipts and sending tickets to the kitchen even with the internet down. A few things that experience taught me about when the web is enough:

The browser handled offline data well. Oscar keeps its data in a local WatermelonDB database on browser storage, so the POS works the same with or without a connection, and nobody has to install anything. Changes sync to a Django backend when the connection returns, and the server stays the source of truth for reporting. I wrote more about that architecture in Offline-First POS: Lessons From Building Oscar in React.

Real-time features need an offline plan of their own. Orders reached the kitchen display system over WebSockets. Every feature like that needs a decision, made at design time, about what happens when the socket drops.

Hardware was the hard part. Restaurants need receipt, kitchen and bar printers. Oscar connects to local printers through QZ Tray, a printer bridge, and I built the routing so each ticket lands on the right printer: receipts at the counter, tickets in the kitchen, drinks at the bar. That pattern (a web app plus a local helper for hardware) is a useful middle ground, but it is one more component to set up and support.

The broader lesson: Oscar ran on counters and devices the business controlled, in the foreground, all shift long. That is the ideal case for a web app. A consumer app that must wake up in the background on a stranger's iPhone is the opposite case.

Answer these honestly. If most of your answers land on the left, a PWA (or a plain responsive web app) is probably the right first build.

For most early-stage products, start on the web. A well-built responsive web app with a manifest and a service worker covers desktop, Android and most iPhone use, can be found on Google, and costs less to build and maintain than separate native apps. If you hit a real platform wall (background work, hardware, iOS push at scale), you can add a React Native app later and reuse your backend, API and much of your business logic.

The mistake to avoid is choosing a PWA and then discovering the iOS gaps after launch. Write down the device features your product depends on, check each one against current browser support, and prototype the riskiest one first.

If you are planning an offline-first app or a POS and want a second opinion on web vs native, take a look at my product development service or the React development service, or see how the Oscar POS case study handled it.

I'm Muhammad Moiz, a full-stack developer who builds web apps, SaaS and POS systems, and takes AI-built apps (Lovable, Bolt, Replit) to production. Get in touch.

#9561. Full App Backup for Game Receipts: Node.js Nightly Job, User Uploads, Object Storage

Short answer: treat a nightly game-app backup as one recoverable run containing the database dump, the original receipt files, and a manifest that names both; use private object storage, immutable run prefixes, and a restore drill before calling the job complete.

The important decision is access control versus delivery simplicity. Receipt images and purchase records are related evidence, not two independent exports. A public object URL may be easy for a client to consume, but it is a poor default for audit material. A private bucket with short-lived, server-issued access takes more application work and gives the recovery process a boundary worth defending.

This is the invariant: a run is either a candidate for restore or it is not. A scheduler success message is not evidence. A database dump that finished while the upload archive was still being assembled is not a backup.

Give every run a unique UTC identifier, and put that identifier in every key. For example:

The prefix is not a folder abstraction that makes consistency appear by magic. It is a naming contract. backups/production/20260811T020000Z/ should contain the database export, the receipt archive, and a manifest only after both payloads have been validated and stored. Keep the environment in the path so an operator cannot confuse staging evidence with production evidence during a stressful recovery.

The manifest should record the run ID, the exact object keys, byte counts, checksums produced by the backup worker, and the database export timestamp. It should also say which upload inventory the archive represents. That last field matters: a receipt row may exist in the database while its original object is absent, or the reverse may be true after a failed deletion workflow.

Short rule: no manifest, no restore candidate.

There is a consistency limit here. A nightly snapshot normally has a point-in-time boundary for the database, but user uploads arrive continuously. Decide what “complete” means before writing code: for example, include every receipt whose database record was committed before the export cutoff, and record any later objects for the next run. The exact policy depends on the application’s transaction model. I’m not sure a single archive can prove that relationship by itself; the manifest and an application-level inventory check are what make the claim testable.

The write path should have four states: planned, payloads stored, manifest committed, and verified. Only the third state is eligible for restore, and only the fourth should trigger retention cleanup. This gives operators a clear failure boundary when a worker is killed halfway through a large archive.

I would choose the third row for the game receipt workflow and keep the bucket private. The catch is that it is not suitable when the primary requirement is anonymous, permanent delivery of public media; a public distribution store or a separate delivery path is the better boundary there. Do not make the backup copy carry that convenience requirement.

Object storage also does not answer every durability question. The bucket may be durable while the design still has one failure domain, one credential, or one region. If the recovery objective includes a regional disaster, create and test a secondary-copy process. If the audit requirement includes immutability, select storage controls and permissions that prevent the backup identity from deleting its own evidence. The capability has to be verified against the actual policy, not inferred from the word “backup” in a product screen.

The storage client is deliberately abstract in this example. The application should bind put_bytes to the chosen object-storage SDK or HTTP implementation, while keeping the ordering and key contract unchanged. This is the part worth testing.

The manifest write is the publication step. A failed payload write must fail the job and leave no manifest; a failed manifest write must not be converted into a success by a scheduler wrapper. Retry policy belongs in the storage adapter, with bounded retries and logs that include the run ID but never receipt contents or credentials.

Before this function runs, the worker still needs a scheduler lock or queue policy so two nightly workers cannot claim the same run. Object keys are useful identifiers, but they are not a substitute for coordination. The job should also retain its local temporary files until the remote objects have been checked, then remove them according to the host’s disk policy.

A restore test should run against an isolated database and an isolated object-storage prefix. The sequence is intentionally boring:

The sixth check is where delivery simplicity gets challenged. A file that can be downloaded by a storage administrator is not necessarily accessible to the audit service, and a file that the audit service can read is not necessarily safe to expose to a game client. Test both authorization decisions. For browser delivery, use an application-controlled, time-limited access mechanism rather than turning the backup prefix into a public asset path.

The rejected design is a single latest/ prefix updated by independent database and upload jobs. It is valid for disposable exports where a new artifact replaces the old one and no relational reference must be reconstructed. It is not suitable for a full app restore: a timeout after the database upload can leave a fresh dump next to yesterday’s receipts, and a successful listing can still tell no one whether the pair is complete.

Lifecycle expiration can remove old run prefixes, but lifecycle configuration is retention automation, not a restore test. Keep a retention review that asks which manifests are complete, which copies are in the secondary location, and which restore drills still meet the recovery objective. Storage pricing also varies by storage class, request type, retrieval, and transfer; cost should be measured from the workload rather than used as the primary architectural argument.

If the access policy, inventory semantics, or disaster-recovery target cannot be stated in one page, the backup design is not finished. More automation will not repair an undefined restore boundary.

#9558. Claude Fable 5.2 vs Opus 5.5: Is Is 2 the price worth it

Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 on November 9. It's the new top of the Claude lineup, aimed at the hardest coding and reasoning work, and it costs twice as much per token as Claude Opus 5.5.

So the useful question isn't "is it better?" Anthropic's own numbers say it usually is. The question is when it's worth 2× the price, and what changes in your code if you switch.

This post covers what's new, the real price difference, the API details that will bite you on migration, and a simple way to decide. Everything here comes from Anthropic's announcement and docs unless it says otherwise.

Anthropic positions Fable 5.2 for "demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work". Compared with Fable 5.1, Anthropic says it:

There's also Claude Mythos 5.2, the same underlying model without the cybersecurity and biology safeguards. It's limited to organisations in Anthropic's verification programs, so for most developers, Fable 5.2 is the one you'll use.

These are from Anthropic's launch table, run at each model's highest effort with Fable's safeguards on. They're lab-reported, not independent, so treat them as a starting point for your own evals.

Two things stand out. The jump from Fable 5.1 is large on long agentic tasks. And Opus 5.5 still wins one row, AA-Briefcase Elo, so "newer and pricier" doesn't mean better at everything.

Fable 5.2 is cheaper than Fable 5.1 was ($10 / $50), but still exactly double Opus 5.5 per token. Batch requests are 50% off on both. Fable also has a fast mode at $16 / $80 that Anthropic says runs up to 2.5× faster.

Per token isn't the whole story, though. A stronger model can finish a task in fewer turns and with fewer retries, so it can cost less per task even at a higher per-token price. That's why the number to track is cost per successful task, not cost per token.

Both models have adaptive thinking always on, and you control how hard they think with the effort parameter. But their defaults are different: Fable 5.2 defaults to high, Opus 5.5 to medium.

So if you compare them with no settings, you're comparing Fable thinking harder against Opus thinking less. Some of the quality gap, and a lot of the cost gap, comes from that alone.

This type-checks against @anthropic-ai/sdk 1.8.0. Two notes on it:

Allowed effort values are low, medium, high, xhigh and max. Anthropic's advice for Fable 5.2: start at high, try xhigh for the hardest long-running work once you've measured a gain, and keep max for testing the ceiling.

If you're swapping the model ID in existing code, check these first. Each one is from the Fable 5.2 docs:

Anthropic's own model guide is refreshingly direct: start with Opus 5.5 for most workloads, and use Fable 5.2 for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work, or when Opus 5.5 at higher effort still falls short on your evals.

In practice, that gives you a simple test:

If Fable passes tasks Opus fails, or finishes in fewer turns, it can pay for itself. If both pass, Opus at half the price is the better default.

We gave both models the exact same prompt and recorded them side by side. [EDITOR: add the prompt, the effort setting used for each model, and 2–3 sentences on what you saw, then link the reel. Don't add numbers you didn't measure.]

One prompt isn't an eval, so treat it as a first impression, not a verdict.

New models will keep arriving every few months. The part that lasts is having your own evals and a workflow that doesn't depend on any single model. If you want to build that workflow properly, it's what our Agentic Engineering course is about.

Which model are you running as your default right now, and what would make you switch?

Sources: Anthropic: Claude Fable 5.2 · Claude docs: Models overview · Claude docs: Effort · Claude docs: Fable 5.2 overview · MacRumors: Anthropic launches Claude Fable 5.2

#9557. How I Learned to Share Ownership With My Product Manager

I’m an experienced product designer who loves science and the human side of technology ⭐️

I’m an experienced product designer who loves science and the human side of technology ⭐️

I’m an experienced product designer who loves science and the human side of technology ⭐️

Building a creative partnership takes more than putting two strong specialists on the same project.

You can be a brilliant designer, an experienced analyst, or a product manager who seems to have an answer for everything. Working with other people can amplify your expertise—or make it surprisingly difficult to put it to use.

I have spent seven years at Yandex, working alongside highly capable people. I have also watched misunderstandings between those people turn straightforward tasks into complicated negotiations.

Expertise does not automatically make collaboration easier. Sometimes, it gives each person more reasons to believe they are right.

I learned that lesson through a conflict I helped create.

While working at Yandex Market, I often took the lead in my partnership with a product manager. I answered product questions, defended our decisions, and proposed alternatives.

My partner seemed less experienced to me. He needed more time to gather his thoughts, while I was quick to jump into a discussion. So I decided, on behalf of both of us, that I would do the talking.

From my perspective, I was helping us move faster.

Eventually, we had a conflict. Through several conversations, I realized that taking over was making him less confident. He had fewer opportunities to explain his reasoning and demonstrate his expertise. I interpreted his hesitation as a reason to step in again.

We discussed what each of us needed. He wanted to present and defend the product rationale himself. I wanted design considerations to have a meaningful place in the decisions.

We changed how we approached product reviews, introduced regular one-on-ones, and became more attentive to each other’s needs within the project.

The problem had never been a shortage of ideas. I had assumed that my way of contributing worked for both of us.

That experience made me revisit my earlier work in advertising agencies, where projects often revolved around a creative pair. Two specialists brought different strengths and developed ideas together. When the partnership worked, they could produce strong work quickly.

I started applying that approach more deliberately to product management and design.

Of course, a PM and designer are part of a larger team. Engineers, analysts, researchers, and other colleagues shape the outcome. But this particular partnership influences many early decisions: which problem to solve, what to explore, and what to test.

I recognize three recurring patterns. These are working dynamics, not fixed personality types.

The PM defines the problem, chooses a solution, and sets the pace. The designer joins when something needs to be drawn.

Work moves forward, but the team uses only part of the designer’s expertise. Questions about usability and alternative approaches arrive too late to influence the direction.

A useful change is to involve design while the problem is still being framed. The designer also needs to bring questions and proposals into that conversation.

The designer takes over framing, strategy, discussions, and presentations. The PM becomes less visible, while the designer accumulates responsibility.

Important tasks can fall through the cracks: who is coordinating with stakeholders, checking business assumptions, or deciding the scope of a release?

Clear ownership helps, provided both people respect it. If your partner owns part of a discussion, leave them time to respond— even when you already have an answer.

Each person can lead, question assumptions, and make room for the other’s expertise.

The designer might help turn an abstract request into a concrete problem. The PM might bring evidence or constraints that change the design direction.

Both need to be willing to adjust. A partnership cannot depend on one person doing all the adapting.

Compromise is sometimes necessary. Deadlines and resources are real, and not every disagreement needs a new workshop.

But I try to avoid settling too quickly for a solution where each person gives something up just to end the argument.

Stephen Covey’s idea of synergy and the third alternative offers a useful way to think about this: different perspectives can help people develop a solution that improves on their original proposals.

Consider a hypothetical disagreement. A PM wants to launch a complex flow quickly. The designer believes the proposed shortcuts will make it confusing.

They could remove a few screens and ship something that satisfies neither concern particularly well.

Or they could examine what the deadline is meant to achieve. If the immediate goal is to test one assumption, a smaller, focused experiment might provide the evidence without requiring the full flow.

That possibility only emerges when both people explain what matters to them and are willing to reconsider their approach.

For me, this is the most valuable part of a creative partnership: discovering an option neither person brought into the room.

A few habits help turn that intention into everyday work.

Earlier in my career, I often entered discussions with an answer ready. Now, I try to establish a shared understanding first:

These questions help the PM clarify the request and help me focus my effort.

Agree on who gathers evidence, coordinates with stakeholders, presents each part of the proposal, and follows up on open questions.

For me, the difficult part was honoring those agreements when I felt tempted to step in.

A productive meeting can still leave two people with different plans. Keep a short record of what you decided, why, who owns the next step, and what remains unresolved. If you defer an improvement, record what would trigger revisiting it.

An art director once told me brainstorming was a waste of time. I have repeatedly found that an hour of focused discussion can accomplish more than a week of messages. Bring a specific question and options to compare. Leave with a decision or a next step.

“You push too hard” gives someone little guidance.

A more useful formulation identifies the behavior, its impact, and a request: “When you answer questions about my work before I can respond, I lose the opportunity to explain my reasoning. Can I lead that part next time?”

That is an illustrative example, but the principle is practical: describe something the other person can recognize and change.

Project meetings tend to fill up with project problems. Regular one-on-ones create space to discuss the working relationship itself.

What went well? What was frustrating? Where did either person need more support? What should we try differently?

Positive feedback matters here, too. Your partner should know which contributions helped. These conversations require participation from both people. One person cannot maintain a healthy partnership alone.

Over the couple of years since I started practicing this approach, I have changed how I work.

I used to spend much more energy defending my ideas and proving my independence. I took on responsibility and found it difficult to share.

Now, I pay closer attention to each person’s strengths. I explain what I can contribute and where I can help. We work out where to combine our efforts and where to trust each other to lead. Our ideas have become stronger, and I have maintained good relationships with my team through large, difficult projects.

I still disagree, ask questions, and stand up for what I believe matters. I am not trying to be the perfect or most agreeable colleague. I want the people around me to have room to do their best work—and to build something together that none of us could have created alone.

The Poirot Method: How Designers Can Investigate Ambiguous Problems
