#9555. How to chase an unpaid invoice in Australia without losing the client (3 message templates)

Chasing an unpaid invoice feels awkward, especially when the client is someone you want to keep. The good news is that most late payments are not deliberate. Invoices get lost in an inbox, sent to the wrong person, or sit in an accounts queue. A short, polite, well-timed message fixes most of them.

This is the three-step approach I suggest for Australian sole traders and small businesses: a friendly nudge, a clear ask, then a firm but fair final reminder. Copy the templates, replace the [brackets], and send them by SMS or email.

A lot of delays come from the invoice, not the client. Before sending any reminder, check that:

Hi [Name], I think tax invoice [#] for $amount, due [date], may have slipped through. Could you check when it will be paid? Bank details are on the invoice. Thanks! [Your name]

Now you ask for a date, and you make it easy to say yes.

Subject: Invoice [#] - $[amount], now [x] days overdue

Hi [Name], I am following up on invoice [#] for $amount, now [x] days past our agreed [14]-day terms. I have attached it again in case the first one went to spam, and our ABN [ABN] is on it. Please pay by [date] or let me know what is holding it up. If something on the invoice is wrong, tell me and I will fix it today.

This one is direct but still professional. Do not threaten, and do not mention fees or formal steps unless they are in your signed terms.

Subject: Final reminder - invoice [#] for $[amount]

Hi [Name], I have not had a reply to my last two messages about invoice [#] for $amount. I would like to settle this without further steps, so please pay in full by [date] or call me on [phone] to agree a payment date. Until it is paid I will have to pause any new work. I would rather keep working together, so a quick reply is all I need.

I put together a free one-page version of these three messages, and a bigger Invoice Reminder Kit with more templates for before-the-due-date nudges, final notices, payment plans, disputes and a 30-day chase calendar. They are written in plain Australian English for tradies, cleaners, freelancers and other small operators. You can find the kits here: https://payhip.com/AussieSmallBizKits

If you use these templates and have a version that works better for you, I would like to hear it in the comments.

This platform not only stands out from the multitude of existing AI tools but also brings a fresh approach to content generation. As we explore LimeWire, our aim is to uncover its features, benefits for creators, and the exciting possibilities it offers for AI content generation. Let's unravel the distinctive features that set LimeWire apart in the dynamic landscape of AI-powered tools, understanding how creators can leverage its capabilities to craft unique and engaging AI-generated images.


Introduction


LimeWire, a name once associated with the notorious file-sharing tool from the 2000s, has undergone a significant transformation. The LimeWire we discuss today is not the file-sharing application of the past but has re-emerged as an entirely new entity—a cutting-edge AI content publishing platform.

This revamped LimeWire invites users to register and unleash their creativity by crafting original AI content, which can then be shared and showcased on the LimeWire Studio. Notably, even acclaimed artists and musicians, such as Deadmau5, Soulja Boy, and Sean Kingston, have embraced this platform to publish their content in the form of NFT music, videos, and images.


Beyond providing a space for content creation and sharing, LimeWire introduces monetization models to empower users to earn revenue from their creations. This includes avenues such as earning ad revenue and participating in the burgeoning market of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs). As we delve further, we'll explore these monetization strategies in more detail to provide a comprehensive understanding of LimeWire's innovative approach to content creation and distribution.


LimeWire Studio welcomes content creators into its fold, providing a space to craft personalized AI-focused content for sharing with fans and followers. Fans have the opportunity to subscribe to creators' pages, immersing themselves in the creative journey and gaining ownership of digital collectibles that hold tradeable value within the LimeWire community. LimeWire AI Studio

AI Image Generation Tools

Much like other tools in the generative AI landscape, LimeWire provides a range of options catering to various levels of complexity in image creation. What sets LimeWire apart is its seamless integration of different AI models and design styles. Excitingly, LimeWire is actively developing its proprietary AI model, signaling ongoing innovation and enhancements to its image generation capabilities. This upcoming addition holds the promise of further expanding the creative horizons for LimeWire users, making it an evolving and dynamic platform within the landscape of AI-driven art and image creation.

This transformative step imbues your artwork with a unique digital signature, securing its authenticity and ownership in the decentralized realm.

In conclusion, LimeWire emerges as a democratizing force in the creative landscape, providing an inclusive platform where anyone can unleash their artistic potential and effortlessly share their work. With the integration of AI, LimeWire eliminates traditional barriers, empowering designers, musicians, and artists to publish their creations and earn revenue with just a few clicks.

#9552. Your MRR Has a Ceiling, and Churn Sets It

I am the founder of Groundwork (https://groundworkblog.com), on the economics of running a software business alone.

I am the founder of Groundwork (https://groundworkblog.com), on the economics of running a software business alone.

I am the founder of Groundwork (https://groundworkblog.com), on the economics of running a software business alone.

A common story among solo SaaS founders goes like this. Growth is steady for a year. Then it slows, then it stalls, even though signups have not dropped. The founder concludes that marketing has stopped working and starts looking for a new channel.

Very often marketing is working exactly as well as before. The business has simply reached the ceiling its churn rate allows, and no new channel changes where that ceiling is unless it changes one of two numbers.

Each month, two things happen to your monthly recurring revenue. New customers add some amount, call it N. Existing customers cancel, removing a share of current MRR equal to your monthly churn rate, c.

Early on, N is much bigger than the churn loss, so MRR climbs. But the churn loss grows with MRR, while N stays roughly flat. Eventually they meet. When the amount you lose each month equals the amount you add, MRR stops moving:

Your MRR ceiling is the new MRR you add each month divided by your monthly churn rate.

Say you add $600 of new MRR every month and lose 4% of your MRR to churn each month.

You will never get past $15,000 MRR with those two numbers, no matter how long you wait. Here is how you approach it, starting from zero:

Two things stand out. Growth looks healthy for the first year, then slows every month after, without anything changing in the business. And at 4% monthly churn, you lose about 39% of your customers every year, which is why the curve bends so early.

The slowdown is gradual, so it looks like a trend in the market rather than a property of your numbers. Month to month, the gain shrinks:

At $5,000 MRR, you gain $600 - $200 = $400. At $10,000 you gain $600 - $400 = $200. At $14,000 you gain $40. Same signups, same marketing, ever-smaller net growth.

Before you change channels, run the check:

If your current MRR is already close to that number, more of the same marketing will not move you much. You are not stalling; you are arriving.

The formula only has two inputs, so there are only two levers.

Raise N. Double your new MRR to $1,200 a month, and the ceiling doubles to $30,000. You can do it with more customers, or with the same number of customers at a higher price. A price rise counts here: if churn does not change, raising the price of new plans raises N, and the ceiling moves with it.

Lower c. Halve churn to 2%, and the ceiling also doubles, to $30,000. But the two levers are not equivalent, because lowering churn changes how fast you get there.

At 4% churn, you reach half your ceiling in about 17 months. At 2% it takes about 34 months, because the ceiling is twice as high and you are filling it at the same rate. Lower churn is the bigger prize, but it is a slow one. The first year looks almost identical.

For a one-person business, the levers cost very different things.

Raising N through acquisition usually costs time or money every single month, forever. Stop the marketing and N falls, and so does the ceiling.

Lowering churn tends to be a one-off fix that keeps paying: an onboarding step that gets new users to the useful part faster, annual plans, a cancellation flow that offers a pause instead of an exit, fixing the bug that makes your most active users leave. Each of those keeps working after you stop thinking about it.

Raising the price is the one move that raises N without more acquisition effort, which is why it is so often the cheapest change available.

A useful habit is to put the ceiling on your dashboard next to MRR. When the two numbers are far apart, growth is mostly a matter of time. When they converge, it is time to change N or c, and the formula tells you how much each change is worth before you spend a week on it.

#9550. Solving the Erasure / Receipt Trilemma in AI Memory and RAG

Why delete_all(user_id=...) breaks GDPR compliance in practice — and how length-prefixed salted Merkle documents, two-tier AES-256-GCM crypto-shredding, and two-direction benchmarks close the gap.

Most vector stores (Qdrant, Chroma, Pinecone, pgvector) and agent memory layers (Mem0, Letta, LangMem) make storing facts and scoping simple queries by user_id straightforward. When a user invokes GDPR Article 17 ("Right to be Forgotten") or an enterprise client demands verifiable offboarding, three failure modes appear silently:

Failure 1: The Erasure / Receipt Trilemma

Imagine an onboarding call transcript or clinical intake note containing facts about two people:

"Priya Raman joined Acme in 2019 as a logistics analyst. Marcus Webb owns a bookshop in Leeds." Your RAG pipeline indexes that transcript and gives Marcus a cryptographic provenance receipt binding his fact to the document's flat SHA-256 hash and UTF-8 byte offsets.

Now Priya requests erasure. A flat document hash forces an impossible trilemma:

Redact or delete the transcript -> Priya's data is gone, but Marcus's SHA-256 receipt breaks forever because both the document digest and every byte offset shifted. Keep the transcript intact so Marcus's receipt verifies -> Priya's PII stays on disk permanently. Failure 2: Derived & Cross-Bucket Memory Leaks

Suppose an agent synthesizes a weekly summary:

"Riverside handoff: triage routing pairs with pharmacy inventory." Because summaries belong to "team_acme" rather than "priya", calling delete_all(user_id="priya") deletes Priya's raw memories — and leaves derived summaries, graph links, and append-only audit logs surfacing her context under a team namespace.

Failure 3: Zombie Re-Ingestion and Fake Compliance Metrics

Zombie syncs (webhook retries, backup imports, stale ETL jobs) re-ingest Priya minutes later under slightly different normalization ("Priya Raman" vs "priya"). Trivial 0-leak metrics: Any benchmark that only measures "leak rate" rewards wiping everything — destroying innocent bystanders' memories alongside the erased subject gives 0 leaks on paper while corrupting your store.

Ember (ember-custody) wraps an existing store (Mem0, LangChain/Chroma/Qdrant vector stores, or SQLite) without rewriting your retrieval model:

A. Salted Length-Prefixed RFC 6962 Merkle Documents (merkle.py)

Instead of hashing the whole document flatly, Ember splits a source into sentence/line/custom leaves, generates a fresh 128-bit random nonce per leaf, and hashes:

leaf_hash = SHA-256(0x00 || uint32_be(len(nonce)) || nonce || leaf_bytes) node_hash = SHA-256(0x01 || left_32 || right_32) Length-prefixing nonce prevents boundary ambiguity between (nonce, text) and ("", nonce + text). RFC 6962 0x00 vs 0x01 domain separation + strict positional proof-walk checks block second-preimage tree-geometry spoofing. On erasure: Ember strips Priya's leaf text and nonce, retaining only Priya's leaf_hash. The tree root stays identical, offline dictionary confirmation on common sentences fails (nonce is gone), and Marcus's receipt still verifies bit-for-bit against the redacted document using zero external dependencies (verify.py). B. Zero-Plaintext Append-Only Ledger + Two-Tier Crypto-Shredding (keystore.py, vault.py)

Append-only SQLiteLedger (WAL, synchronous=FULL) hashes an unbroken SHA-256 chain over encrypted subjects, text, quote, and caller metadata (AES-256-GCM bound via AAD to (tenant_id, item_id, field, key_ref)). Direct records encrypt under an opaque subject CEK (subject:subj_). Shared and derived_from records automatically compute the transitive ancestor set of all contributors and encrypt under a tracked per-record DEK (record:) indexed under every contributing subject. Erasing Priya redacts shared source leaves and destroys both Priya's CEK and every derived/shared DEK before calling external vendor delete() (so even a network timeout never leaves local decryption keys alive, and retries safely sweep pending IDs). From-zero ledger replay remains 100% tamper-evident while yielding [erased] and {} for all of Priya's items — leaving innocent bystanders decrypted and retrievable. C. Keyed Tombstones & Two-Direction Calibration (reducer.py, audit.py)

Vault-keyed HMAC-SHA256 tombstones block zombie re-ingestion with TombstonedSubjectError unless an explicit reconsent_id is recorded. erase() probes the raw backing store directly (adapter.search()) and refuses to issue an Ed25519 ErasureCertificate (ErasureIncomplete) if any residue still surfaces. The built-in adversarial suite tests 12 subjects × 7 attack categories (204 probes) while co-gating bystander retrieval survival and redacted Merkle receipt verification: Naive user_id-only baseline: 204/204 probes leak Ember wrapper: 0/204 probes leak, 100% bystander memories survive, 100% bystander receipts verify offline, 100% from-zero replays stay content-free.

Cryptography cannot erase data you already leaked out-of-band. Every certificate explicitly records trust boundaries (trust_boundary in ErasureCertificate):

Separate your keys from ledger backups: Crypto-shredding only protects pre-existing snapshots if key_dir (or your KMS/HSM KeyStore) was never backed up alongside ledger.db. External timestamp anchoring: Without configuring a TimestampAnchor (RFC 3161 TSA or public transparency log), a malicious root operator holding both ledger.db and ed25519.json can rewrite history coherently. Unanchored certificates explicitly declare externally_timestamped: false. Unlinked copy-paste residue: Structural lineage catches everything written via subjects and derived_from plus optional leaf_predicate sweeps; unlinked copies still trigger fail-closed rejection via probes.

#9548. How to Get Free Devnet SOL in 2026 (and Why solana airdrop Fails Now)

Posted on Nov 11 • Originally published at solstack.xyz

Most Solana tutorials still start the same way: install the CLI, make a keypair, run solana airdrop 2. Run that against devnet today (CLI 4.2.2 here) and you get this:

The message blames a rate limit, so the natural move is to wait and try again later. For us it failed the same way a day later. We ran into this while funding test wallets for our own tools, and the cause turned out to be something waiting can't fix.

The CLI's airdrop command is a thin wrapper around one RPC method, requestAirdrop. Call that method yourself and the node gives a much clearer answer:

HTTP 410, Gone: the RPC faucet is closed on this cluster. Both api.devnet.solana.com and api.testnet.solana.com gave that answer on 11 November 2026. web3.js 1.99.0 hits the same wall, because connection.requestAirdrop() sends the same call:

So the airdrop built into the public RPC is switched off. A setup script or a test suite that asks the public endpoint for SOL stops at that line, and it will keep stopping there until the SOL comes from somewhere else.

Three ways to get test SOL still work. Which one fits depends on whether you're clicking through an app in a browser or running code.

A web faucet is a page that sends devnet SOL to an address out of a wallet somebody keeps funded. We run one, the Solstack Devnet Faucet, so people can try our tools on devnet before they spend real SOL.

The SOL shows up a few seconds later, with a Solscan link to the transfer. When we timed a request on 11 November it came back in 4.8 seconds. Each wallet address, and each IP, gets one request every 8 hours.

The whole request on video, in one minute:

The Solana Foundation runs a web faucet too, at the address the RPC error points to. Its page lists a maximum of 2 requests every 8 hours, and a higher limit if you sign in with GitHub.

If it's code that needs the SOL, and especially if that code runs in CI, skip devnet. The CLI ships with solana-test-validator, a single-node cluster on your own machine whose faucet has no rate limit:

That's the command that fails on devnet, and here it hands over 100 SOL in one go. requestAirdrop works from web3.js as well once the connection points at http://127.0.0.1:8899.

A local validator starts out empty, though. Your own program has to be deployed to it, and anything you rely on from devnet has to be copied in when it starts:

Tests that used to open with a devnet airdrop are better off here anyway. They stop depending on a faucet that somebody else can close.

Devnet SOL moves like any other SOL. If a teammate has some, or another wallet of yours does, one transfer covers it:

The last flag is needed because the CLI won't send to an address that holds no SOL unless you tell it to. This is how we fund the throwaway wallets in our own test runs: one funded wallet pays the rest.

A long way. Fees on devnet are the same as on mainnet: 5,000 lamports per signature, and a new token account takes a deposit of 1,488,440 lamports, about 0.0015 SOL. One SOL covers that deposit for roughly 670 token accounts.

For a sense of scale, on 10 November we ran our tools end to end on devnet. That run created a token, burned some of it, locked some, sent two multisends, opened two liquidity pools, added and removed liquidity, and launched a coin on a launchpad. All of it used about 0.55 SOL.

Devnet SOL has no value and can't be moved to mainnet, and the network can be reset, so there's little point in stockpiling it.

A faucet is a server that holds a funded keypair and signs a transfer when asked. The core of ours is a few lines in a Cloudflare Worker:

One bug from ours might save you some time. The first version waited for the transfer with connection.confirmTransaction(). That call listens on a WebSocket subscription, and inside a Worker the subscription never answered. The SOL landed in about a second. The request then sat there until the blockhash expired, roughly 38 seconds later, and reported "Send failed" for a transfer that had gone through.

The same request now answers in three to five seconds. On any serverless runtime, check that your confirmation step doesn't need a socket to stay open.

You'll also want a limit per address and per IP, or a single script will empty the wallet.

With SOL in the wallet, devnet is the place to rehearse anything you'd pay for on mainnet. Creating a token, sending an airdrop to a list and opening a liquidity pool all work there the way they do on mainnet.

#9547. 51 Thanksgiving dessert recipes for a sweet holiday: From cookies to cake — and of course, plenty of pie.

Of course, we had to start with pumpkin pie. This is a rich, well-spiced pie, thanks to a powerful punch of ginger, cinnamon, nutmeg, cloves, and black pepper. Two hints for a better result: Mix the filling a day in advance to give the spices a chance to bloom, and be sure to remove the pie from the oven while the center is still wobbly, as overcooking it will cause the filling to crack.

Want even more spice in your pumpkin pie? This spice-forward recipe is for you. Using powerful Vietnamese cinnamon — with its more robust flavor profile — gives the pie an even spicier kick. Meanwhile, the filling is super silky-smooth thanks to a few tablespoons of corn syrup mixed in.

Get the recipe: Smooth and Spicy Pumpkin Pie

With its retro vibe, this play on classic chiffon pie is noteworthy for its tender rye crust and its bright, light chiffon filling. The zesty cranberry curd and smooth, sweet Swiss meringue play beautifully together. And the gelatin helps the filling set just right so that once refrigerated, the pie can be sliced neatly. Tart and airy, this pie is an excellent counterpoint to a heavy feast.

Shop the recipe: Organic Medium Rye Flour

Intimidated by pie? Don't be! Our guide on How to Bake Pie has everything you need for a successful, stress-free bake.

This double-crusted beauty is generously filled with sweet-tart apples and spiced with cinnamon, nutmeg, and allspice. But the real secret to its flavorful filling is boiled cider, one of our favorite fall ingredients. The sticky tart-sweet syrup adds an extra depth of apple flavor to make this classic pie stand out from the crowd.

Shop the recipe: Vermont Boiled Cider and Instant ClearJel

This unusual method for baking apple pie caught our eye years ago, when a reader sent it via e-mail. But it’s not just a stunt: Baking a pie in a paper grocery bag gives you a beautifully golden brown, perfectly cooked pie, with toothsome yet tender apples (which soften better thanks to the steam trapped by the bag) beneath a streusel topping.

This beloved pie is made much like pumpkin pie, but with mashed sweet potatoes for nuanced flavor and heavy cream for an especially rich custard. Top it with toasted molasses meringue (if you want the pie to be reminiscent of the classic yams and marshmallow dish served at Thanksgiving), or for a simpler option, with freshly whipped cream. (And for a more unconventional version, try this striking Purple Sweet Potato Pie.)

This traditional pie doesn’t use corn syrup — instead, it’s sweetened entirely with brown sugar. The filling is silky smooth, and the pecans on top toast nicely as the pie bakes. Be sure to use high-quality vanilla extract for well-rounded flavor; an optional handful of chopped bittersweet chocolate is a nice addition, too.

If you’re intimidated by pie (or just don’t have time to chill and roll out pie dough) this easier version of pecan pie is for you. A buttery, brown-sugar shortbread crust cradles a gooey honey-sweetened pecan filling. These bars keep well for days, so they’re perfect for baking ahead of Thanksgiving.

This recipe takes classic pecan pie a step further by adding chocolate chips to the filling. The chocolate beautifully complements the pecans' nuttiness; if you choose bittersweet chocolate, it cuts the pie's overall sweetness, allowing all of the flavors to shine more brightly.

Shop the recipe: Guittard Bittersweet Chocolate Chips

Baker's tip: Make and freeze your pie crust early to get ahead on pie prep.

This creamy, decadent pie is positively bursting with maple flavor — be sure to use the best maple syrup you can find and a dash of natural maple flavor to enhance it. One bite of the brûléed maple sugar top and the silky-smooth filling will have you reconsidering your regular rotation of cream pies this Thanksgiving.

Shop the recipe: Vermont Maple Syrup and Natural Maple Flavor

These handheld treats harness all the nostalgia of a steaming hot McDonald’s fried apple pie but are infinitely better, thanks to homemade flaky pie crust, a fresh apple filling amplified by boiled cider, and a generous coating of cinnamon sugar. If you’re only in charge of dessert this year and want to flex a little, this recipe is an impressive (and tasty!) way to do so.

Shop the recipe: Boiled Cider and Apple Pie Spice

Mash-up pies are an easy way to please your guests without making multiple pies. This recipe has the best of both worlds: a smooth layer of spiced pumpkin custard plus a rich pecan topping. It’s best made a day ahead so that the flavors can settle, plus there’s one less dish to worry about on Thanksgiving Day.

Shop the recipe: Adjustable Pie Crust Shield

Is there anything cuter than a mini Thanksgiving pie? Filled with a pre-cooked, perfectly spiced filling that’s enhanced with tart boiled cider, these bite-sized treats can be topped with a woven lattice or streusel.

This tart-sweet cake is easy to throw together — made with melted butter, the one-bowl batter is mixed by hand then poured directly over sugared cranberries. If you have cranberries leftover from making sauce or just want to highlight these seasonal berries in other ways, make this cake.

Shop the recipe: Pure Almond Extract and Sparkling Sugar

This stunning pumpkin swirl cake is more than just good looks: It also has a soft, plush texture, thanks to cake flour and sour cream, and a deep pumpkin flavor paired with fragrant vanilla. It starts with one base batter that gets flavored two ways, creating two distinct colors for a striking visual contrast when sliced.

For a more traditional dessert, try this pumpkin-y layer cake. It’s moist and slightly dense from the pumpkin purée, with a tangy cream cheese frosting and sticky caramel glaze.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Layer Cake with Cream Cheese Frosting

In this unabashedly apple-forward apple cake, there are so many apple slices and so little batter, you’ll wonder how (and if) it will hold together. But never fear: As the batter rises in the oven, it knits those slices together to create a tender cake that’s almost creamy and custardy due to the abundance of fruit.

Shop the recipe: Almond Flour and Pure Almond Extract

The pumpkin and pumpkin-friendly spices (cloves, cinnamon, allspice) in this cake meld surprisingly well with the chocolate chips studded throughout. This dark, moist Bundt cake is rich enough to serve unfrosted, and it's just the ticket when you want to serve a dessert that's substantial, yet not too sweet, to finish your Thanksgiving meal. And it keeps well for days, so you can bake it early in the week to help prep ahead.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin-Chocolate Chip Cake

This golden cake is rich, moist, and subtly spiced to complement, rather than overshadow, the natural flavor of sweet potatoes. It also includes a crunchy pecan crust on both the top and bottom, along with a touch of maple syrup in the cake for sweetness. If you’re not a fan of pie, this sweet potato cake just may be the perfect Thanksgiving dessert.

Get the recipe: Pecan-Crusted Sweet Potato Pound Cake

With a hidden swirl of coffee-flavored filling, this stunning cake adds an extra dimension to your holiday table. It’s like a pumpkin spice latte in dessert form — and also secretly whole wheat!

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Espresso Bundt Cake

Wondering how far ahead you can make your cake? Here's how long cake lasts in the fridge and at room temp.

This cake is an old favorite of our readers, with over 300 five-star reviews. It's a recipe where the whole is definitely more than the sum of the parts: The moist, semi-chunky cake is packed with four cups of apples, then spread with the frosting equivalent of brown sugar fudge. The whole thing comes together by hand in one bowl, so it also fits easily into your Thanksgiving prep.

Get the recipe: Old-Fashioned Apple Cake with Brown Sugar Frosting

Shop the recipe: Apple Pie Spice and Vermont Boiled Cider

Why decide between cheesecake and pie when you can have both? This eye-catching two-toned recipe pairs custardy pumpkin pie with creamy cheesecake for a dessert that will satisfy everyone.

For an all-pumpkin Thanksgiving cheesecake, there’s this classic version, which transforms pumpkin pie into a silky, velvety filling. Because it needs to chill before serving, this cheesecake is an excellent candidate for baking a day ahead of Thanksgiving.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Cheesecake with Gingersnap Crust

Shop the recipe: Vietnamese Cinnamon, Ginger, and Nutmeg

We did the testing: This is the best way to keep your cheesecake from cracking.

It’s right there in the name: This is an easy, failproof cheesecake that comes together quickly and bakes up beautifully. You don’t even need a water bath! Top with maple- or bourbon-spiked whipped cream to dress it up for the holiday; details are in the recipe tips at the bottom of our Homemade Whipped Cream recipe.

For a fall-forward cheesecake, turn to this seasonal recipe. The texture of the filling is ultra-smooth and creamy, and the maple flavor is apparent, yet subtle — the secret is natural maple flavor paired with maple syrup. The pecan crust, meanwhile, is a nutty, salty counterbalance to the filling.

Shop the recipe: Vermont Maple Syrup and Natural Maple Flavor

If you’re looking for a celebratory yet unexpected dessert for your table, we recommend this recipe. A heavy pour of Irish whiskey cream liqueur (save some for your after-dinner coffee!) flavors the smooth, light filling, while silky chocolate ganache adorns the top. Oven space at a premium while you prep Thanksgiving dinner? This dessert is no-bake, so you can save some room in the cooking schedule.

With its burnished top and custardy interior, this cheesecake reimagines the classic with bold autumnal flair, thanks to golden pumpkin purée and warm spices.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Basque Cheesecake

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

This flourless cake is incredibly rich — like sliceable fudge sauce. A thick icing of chocolate ganache glaze takes it over the top, but if you want something a touch lighter after a heavy Thanksgiving feast, top it instead with a dusting of confectioners’ sugar and a spoonful of barely sweetened whipped cream.

Baker's tip: Make your whipped cream in a Mason jar, especially helpful if you're bringing dessert to someone else's home.

Shop the recipe: Callebaut Semisweet Chocolate Chips

This chocolate pie, with its flaky pastry crust and glistening, ruby-colored cranberry topping, is a non-traditional twist on Thanksgiving flavors. With a semisweet chocolate ganache, nutty whole-grain flour in the crust, and tangy fruit, it delivers a novel and enticing new holiday pie.

This pecan tart recipe is the more lavish, decadent cousin of a classic pecan pie. The pecans are enveloped in a rich, chewy caramel filling, and a blanket of velvety smooth chocolate ganache covers the top of the tart, lending it major candy bar vibes with a touch of sophistication.

Shop the recipe: Guittard Semisweet Chocolate Wafers

This nostalgic pie is the perfect combination of crispy crust, dense chocolatey filling, and ethereal whipped cream. Instead of eggs, this pie relies on cornstarch to bind the gooey filling; coconut cream, meanwhile, stands in for butter. With tons of toasty pecans bound together in a rich, sweet syrup and cradled in a flaky crust, it’s hard to believe this pie is vegan.

#9543. From Booking Requests to Confirmed Bookings: Designing Reliable Server-Side Events

A form submission is easy to track. A confirmed booking is harder.

In booking-based businesses, the customer may submit a request, reserve multiple seats, change plans, or cancel before attending. If all of those actions are counted as conversions, marketing reports can look successful while overstating actual business outcomes.

I worked on this problem in a booking attribution project where the goal was to connect campaign information, booking requests, CRM status changes, and analytics events.

This article describes the event-design decisions and testing approach. The code examples are simplified illustrations, not copies of production code.

The first challenge was semantic, not technical.

These stages are related, but they are not interchangeable.

A request tells us that someone expressed interest. A confirmation tells us that the business secured a booking. Attendance tells us something different again.

The tracking model must preserve those distinctions.

In our project, the primary marketing outcome was a confirmed booking, not simply a form submission.

Rather than sending an indistinguishable conversion every time something changes, define separate event types.

A useful event record might look like this:

This is an illustrative schema, not an actual customer record.

A confirmation should be generated from the actual booking state, not inferred from a thank-you page.

The implementation connects several parts of an existing booking system.

The website captures a request. The booking system remains responsible for booking status. The integration layer turns relevant state changes into analytics events.

This separation matters because marketing tools should not decide whether a customer has been confirmed. That decision belongs to the business system.

The server-side layer can then provide consistent delivery, validation, and retry handling.

Duplicate events are one of the easiest ways to corrupt conversion reporting.

Processing the same business event twice should not produce two business conversions.

For example, an idempotency key can combine the booking ID, transition type, and a transition version:

Conceptually, the server-side processing logic becomes:

The event record and its queue entry should be created reliably together. A retry should reuse the same event identity rather than create a new conversion.

It is also important to distinguish accepted by an API from visible in an analytics report. Those are separate verification steps.

One booking request can cover multiple people.

Suppose a customer requests three seats and the booking is confirmed.

If the dashboard reports three bookings instead of three seats, the result is misleading.

A correct report needs explicit metric definitions.

This is especially important for events, appointments, group activities, and other businesses where one customer action can represent several participants.

Campaign parameters are useful, but they should only be processed and forwarded to analytics platforms when the applicable consent requirements are satisfied.

In this implementation, consent is part of the tracking flow rather than an afterthought.

There is also a difference between knowing the campaign associated with a booking request and identifying the exact Instagram conversation that produced it.

Those are different levels of attribution.

The current system can preserve available campaign information and report booking statuses. It does not establish a verified one-to-one match between every individual Instagram Direct conversation and a specific booking.

Reporting should communicate that boundary instead of implying a level of certainty that the data cannot support.

A successful network request does not prove that the overall tracking implementation is correct.

Testing should cover the complete path from an initial booking request to the final business status.

Test records must also be distinguishable from real business results.

In the real project, some screenshots and counts come from integration tests. They demonstrate configured workflows, not proven increases in customers, sales, or revenue.

A useful conversion-tracking system is not simply one that sends more events.

It is one that answers precise questions:

When these questions are answered, analytics becomes much more useful for operational decisions.

I documented the real project, including implementation screenshots and its current limitations, in this booking attribution case study.

The broader principle applies beyond bookings: track confirmed business outcomes as distinct states, and test the entire data path before trusting a conversion report.

#9542. 17 apple dessert recipes for fall baking: Embrace the season with apple tarts, cookies, cakes, and more.

There’s an apple dessert for everyone. For the purists, there are lattice-topped pies and shingled galettes. For the non-traditionalists, there are caramel-frosted cakes and fritter-inspired loaves. And for apple lovers that hate cinnamon? Well, there are custardy cakes and classic French tarts. Ready to start baking with fall’s best fruit? Read on for our best apple dessert recipes.

There’s no shortage of apple in this cake — applesauce keeps things moist while boiled cider adds sharp, tangy fruit flavor. The cake is great on its own, but pair it with light, creamy Whipped Caramel Frosting, and you’ve got an irresistible baked version of a caramel apple (with none of the fears about your teeth).

Get the recipe: Whipped Caramel Apple Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vermont Boiled Cider

You only need one apple (and two people eager for an apple dessert) to make a pair of these adorable galettes. Half the apple is sliced, while the other half is grated, which creates a hidden layer of jam beneath the shingled slices. Flaky fruit tarts don’t get easier (or cuter!) than this.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

Get the recipe: Apple Cider Snickerdoodles

This super-easy one-bowl cake is loaded with chopped apples and walnuts, which give this moist, spiced cake heft and texture. The frosting, akin to a velvety brown sugar fudge, adds a textural counterpoint and an extra dimension of richness.

Get the recipe: Old-Fashioned Apple Cake with Brown Sugar Frosting

To make this recipe, you'll need: 9" x 13" pan

Cinnamon and apple go together like a flannel and a beanie, but this recipe one-ups that perfect pairing with the addition of cinnamon chips. Diced apple and melty pockets of cinnamon-sugar are also studded throughout these autumnal scones, which are then finished off with an extra-crunchy sugar coating.

Get the recipe: Fresh Apple Cinnamon Scones

To make this recipe, you'll need: Cinnamon Sweet Bits

Ribbons of gooey, cinnamon-scented apples are twisted throughout this striking enriched loaf. Beautiful to behold (and easier to make than you’d think), this braided babka would be a welcome addition to any Rosh Hashanah table or fall celebration.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Baker’s Special Dry Milk

Spoiler alert: The eponymous secret ingredient in this special pie is boiled cider! Made by cooking down apple cider into a concentrate, a few drops deliver big apple flavor. When used in apple pies, it super-charges the fruit’s tart, tangy flavor, delivering a pie with over-the-top apple goodness.

Get the recipe: Secret Ingredient Apple Pie

To make this recipe, you'll need: Boiled Cider

If your go-to doughnut order is an apple fritter, this mash-up cake was made for you. The batter is made using the reverse creaming technique, which ensures a velvety crumb and tender texture. In each slice, there’s a filling and topping of cinnamon-dusted apples and a final drizzle of icy-white vanilla glaze. A slice rivals anything you can get at your local doughnut shop.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Instant ClearJel

This time of year, apples don't need much to make them shine. The paper-thin, crackly top layer of this cobbler highlights the juicy fruit beneath. It doesn’t need a lot of adornment, but a scoop of vanilla ice cream never hurt anything.

Get the recipe: Sugar-Crusted Apple Cobbler Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vietnamese Cinnamon

Is it a bar? A slab pie? Both! This breezy recipe swaps the flaky pastry for a buttery shortbread crust but keeps the warm, gooey apples and classic spices for a sliceable, portable dessert. To finish, there's a crumbly streusel topping inspired by Dutch apple pie.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

When you want a fruit dessert fast, you can always count on crisps — no rolling, no resting, and most importantly, no special equipment required! This crisp is made with a handful of baking basics, so when you find yourself with a surplus of apples, dessert is barely an hour away.

To make this recipe, you'll need: 9" Square Pan

Beneath a buttery, apple-pie-spiced streusel lies a generous layer of tender apples, enriched with intensely flavored boiled cider for a filling that tastes like a truly great apple pie — rich, saucy, and fork-tender apples. The sour cream cake that surrounds the apple filling is plush, subtly tangy, and ultra-moist, providing the perfect counterpoint to the fruit filling and crumb topping.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

If you’re looking to veer from classic apple pie territory, this galette stays true to those roots but adds a few modern twists. It starts with a buttery whole wheat crust enriched with a touch of sour cream. Then, a layer of apple butter (which can be easily made by cooking down applesauce) is spread beneath a layer of artfully arranged apples slices.

Get the recipe: Apple Butter Apple Galette

To make this recipe, you'll need: Sparkling Sugar

There’s just enough batter to hold together a heap of sliced apples in this one-of-a-kind cake. Gently sweetened with brown sugar and scented with almond extract, this minimalist cake is greater than the sum of its parts — a sophisticated, custardy cake that’s deceivingly simple to make.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Almond Extract

This pull-apart bread is as fun to make as it is to eat. After rolling out the dough into a rectangle, it’s spread with sweetened apple filling. The dough is cut up into several strips, then stacked and squeezed into a loaf pan. It bakes into a loaf comprised of distinct slices of pillowy apple-studded bread that you can easily tear from the loaf.

Get the recipe: Cinnamon-Apple Pull-Apart Bread

To make this recipe, you'll need: SAF Instant Yeast

The French know a thing or two about baking with apples, and perhaps no recipe is as classic — or elegant — as the Tarte Tatin. Comprised of deeply caramelized apples layered over buttery pastry, it’s a dessert that stuns. Here, we've tested endlessly to ensure this sometimes-fussy dessert goes off without a hitch in your home kitchen.

Get the recipe: Classic Apple Tarte Tatin

To make this recipe, you'll need: King Arthur Round Cake Pan

These handheld treats harness all the nostalgia of a steaming hot McDonald’s fried apple pie but are infinitely better, thanks to the triple threat of a homemade flaky pie crust, a fresh apple filling amplified by boiled cider, and a generous coating of cinnamon sugar.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Boiled Cider and Apple Pie Spice
